preamble: The development of the voiceless uvular plosive /q/ (Old Arabic qāf) into the voiced alveolar affricate [dz] is a dialect-specific change of central and north-central Arabia. Holes (1991, as summarized by Al-Rojaie 2010) describes three stages: Old Arabic /q/ was fronted and voiced to [g] in Bedouin dialects, [g] was then affricated to [dz] next to front vowels (chiefly /i/), and the affricate was later fronted to dental. It parallels the affrication of /k/ to [ts] in the same communities. Johnstone (1963) and Cantineau (1936–37) found [dz] among tribes along the borders of Najd and north-central Arabia (e.g. Shammar, ʿUtaibah, Muṭair, Dawāsir, Ḍafīr) and in the sedentary speech of Riyadh, ʿUnaizah (Qaṣīm) and Ḥāʾil. Eastern Arabian, Gulf, Mesopotamian and Shawi dialects instead have [dʒ] for the same conditioned reflex, so the [dz] outcome is effectively confined to one Arabic dialect area and is now receding under leveling toward [g]. Commonality is lowered to 2 accordingly.

examples.note: 'really' (lit. 'truth'); one of the words with [dz] in every token
'in front of'; a rare case of [dz] without an adjacent front vowel
'vein'; Al-Rojaie (2010) finds older speakers use [dz] 94% of the time vs. 35% for younger speakers, who favor the regional standard [g]

sources: Mahzari, M. (2023). The Historical Changes of /k/ and /q/ in Najdi Arabic: A Phonological Analysis. Theory and Practice in Language Studies 13(3), 796–807. https://doi.org/10.17507/tpls.1303.30

Al-Rojaie, Y. (2010). The Effect of Social Factors on Sound Change in Najdi Arabic: The Case of [d͡z] in the Qaṣīmī Dialect. Journal of King Saud University: Languages and Translation 22(2), 127–136. https://direct.ksu.edu.sa/handle/ksu-press/1874
